study.title: Romans 3 - The universal guilt and the righteousness of God by faith
study.overview: Romans 3 responds to the objections raised after the comparison between Jews and Gentiles in Romans 2 and leads to the center of the Pauline argument: the whole of mankind is under sin, no one is justified by works of the Law, and the righteousness of God is freely manifested in Jesus Christ, received by faith. The chapter preserves the value of Jewish prerogatives, but shows that such privileges do not nullify human guilt. At the end, Paul concludes that faith does not destroy the Law; rather, it confirms it, because salvation in Christ accomplishes what the Law pointed out and excludes any human boast.

outline.title: The advantages of the Jews and the faithfulness of God
outline.explanation: Paul asks what the advantage of the Jew and answers that is great, especially because the words of God have been entrusted to them. He then anticipates and rejects the objection that human infidelity could cancel divine fidelity. Even when some act with unbelief, God remains true, righteous in his judgment, and unable to be accused of injustice by punishing sin. Paul also rejects the slander that his message would lead to the practice of evil to produce good.

outline.title: Jews and Gentiles under sin
outline.explanation: Paul concludes that neither Jews nor Gentiles are in a superior condition before God: they are all under sin. To support this, he gathers biblical testimonies that describe the corruption of speech, ways and fear of God. The function of the Law in this context is to silence every mouth and make the world blameable before God; it reveals sin, but it produces no justification by works.

outline.title: The righteousness of God in Christ and the faith that confirms the Law
outline.explanation: Now the righteousness of God is presented as something manifested without relying on the works of the Law, although it was already testified by the Law and the Prophets. This righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, reaches Jews and Gentiles, and is founded on the grace of God, in redemption in Christ, and in the sacrifice of reconciliation. Thus, human pride is excluded, justification is by faith and not by works, and God remains the only God who justifies circumcised and uncircumcised. Paul's conclusion is that faith does not nullify the Law, but confirms it.

study.context: The chapter continues the line of argumentation begun in Romans 1-2. The notes highlight that Paul answers real objections to his teaching, especially to the question about the Jewish's advantage and the risk of understanding his message as contempt for the Law. The immediate background is the tension between Jewish privileges and the assertion that Jews and Gentiles are equally under sin. The notes also show that Paul uses a style of question and answer to anticipate resistance to his argument.
study.theology: The central teaching of the chapter is that the saving righteousness of God is not obtained by moral performance or legal observance, but received by faith in Jesus Christ. This does not mean that the Law is useless; rather, it reveals sin, witnesses the righteousness of God and finds its confirmation in the work of Christ. The chapter preserves two truths at the same time: the holiness of God, who judges with truth, and the grace of God, which justifies the sinner freely. It also affirms the universality of sin and salvation: there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles as to the need for redemption, and there is no difference as to the only God who justifies by faith. The cross, understood here as a sacrifice of reconciliation and redemption, demonstrates that God is just in seriously treating sin and, at the same time, justifying him who believes in Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: Paul anticipates the objection that faith without the Law seems to nullify the demands of the Law; however, according to the note, faith really enables people to comply with the Law, for the Holy Spirit is given to those who believe.
The note highlights that, after proving the guilt of Jews and Gentiles, Paul concludes that it is useless to seek justification by the works of the Law; it can only be received by faith.
The note states that faith in Christ does not establish a religion without a Law, but confirms the Law itself by showing that everything is fulfilled in the passion and death of Christ.

questions: If the words of God were entrusted to the Jews, how does this increase their responsibility before God?
What does it mean, in practice, to say that no one is justified by the works of the Law, but by faith in Jesus Christ?
In what ways does faith in Christ confirm the Law rather than destroy it?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to humility. He cuts off all religious advantage and shows that no one can stand before God with his own merit. In practice, this leads us to abandon moral self-confidence, receive with gratitude the grace of Christ and treat Jews and Gentiles - and, by extension, all human groups - as equally in need of mercy. It also calls us to honor the Law of God not as a ladder of merit, but as an instrument that reveals sin and leads us to Christ.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not even detail all verses, so some formulations summarize the flow of the argument from the commented excerpts. There is also not enough base in the notes to state with certainty historical elements beyond what the chapter itself and the comments inform, such as exact circumstances of the Roma community or precise dates.
